CMP Process Handbook — Defect Signatures
Process Step: CMP

1. Donut defects from pad wear

Chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) can produce a Donut defect: a ring-shaped band
of failing die at mid radius. The dominant root cause is polishing pad wear. As the
pad wears unevenly over its lifetime, the material removal rate at the wafer edge
increases relative to the center. The over-polished annular zone manifests as the
donut-shaped defect band. Because the pad is a consumable, this is treated as a
Material type cause, and it is associated with the polish down-force (polish
pressure) running high in the affected zone.

2. Scratch defects from slurry contamination

A second, distinct CMP signature is the Scratch pattern — linear defects that cut
across the wafer surface. The usual cause is slurry particle contamination: when
slurry particles agglomerate, the hardened clumps drag across the wafer during
polishing and gouge linear scratches. This is a Material type cause tied to the
slurry flow parameter.

3. Confirming the causes

For both signatures, polish pressure and slurry flow telemetry should be reviewed.
Pad wear and slurry contamination are both material/consumable issues, so maintenance
history (pad change, slurry lot change) and alarm history are informative. The
normal-lot ratio on the same polisher serves as a negative control, and the yield
change point helps date the onset.

Deposition Defect Catalog
Process Step: DEPO

1. Center defects from gas-flow imbalance

Center-clustered failures on the wafer map are frequently traced back to the
deposition step. When the process gas is not delivered uniformly, the film grows
thicker at the wafer center than at the edge. This center-thick film profile
manifests as a Center defect cluster at electrical test.

The immediate surface cause is gas flow imbalance during deposition: insufficient
precursor gas flow starves the outer radius while the center over-deposits. Because
the imbalance is a process-parameter deviation, it should be treated as a Parameter
type cause, and it is tied to the deposition gas flow parameter running low.

2. Upstream cause: mass flow controller drift

Gas flow imbalance is often not the deepest cause. A frequent upstream driver is
mass flow controller (MFC) drift in the deposition tool. As the MFC drifts out of
calibration, it skews the delivered gas ratios, which in turn produces the flow
imbalance described above. MFC drift is a machine issue and therefore also connects
to the deposition gas flow parameter reading low.

3. Confirming the cause

Deposition gas flow telemetry should be examined for the suspect chamber and time
window. Because MFC drift is a machine fault, maintenance and alarm history for the
tool are useful, and the normal-lot ratio provides a negative control. When the
Center signature is confirmed, the yield change point is worth locating to bound the
onset of the excursion.

Plasma Etch Root-Cause Analysis Guide
Process Step: ETCH

1. Edge-Ring defects and the focus ring

One of the most common edge-related failure signatures in plasma etch is the
Edge-Ring pattern, in which failing die form a continuous band along the wafer
periphery. Field experience shows that focus ring erosion in the etch chamber is
a leading root cause. As the focus ring physically wears down over many RF hours,
plasma confinement at the wafer edge degrades. This degradation typically forces
the tool to compensate with elevated RF power, and the combination produces a
characteristic edge ring defect pattern.

The mechanism is a two-step chain. First, focus ring erosion (a machine/consumable
issue) develops in the chamber. Second, the weakened edge confinement causes etch
rate non-uniformity that is concentrated along the outer ring of the wafer. It is
this etch rate non-uniformity that directly manifests as the Edge-Ring pattern, so
in causal terms the non-uniformity is the surface cause and focus ring erosion is
the deeper root cause behind it.

2. Confirming the cause

When an Edge-Ring signature appears, RF power telemetry for the suspect chamber
should be reviewed first, since elevated RF power is the primary tell. Maintenance
history is equally important: a focus ring that is overdue for replacement is
strong corroborating evidence. Alarm history around the affected time window may
also show plasma-instability events. Finally, the normal-lot ratio on the same
chamber should be checked as a negative control before concluding.

Lithography Field Notes
Process Step: LITHO

1. Edge-Loc defects from focus drift

The Edge-Loc pattern shows failing die localized to one or more sectors of the wafer
edge, rather than a continuous ring. In lithography, a recurring cause is focus drift
near the wafer edge. When the exposure focus drifts away from best focus at the
periphery, the aerial image blurs and the pattern fails locally, yielding localized
edge defects. This should be read as distinct from an Edge-Ring signature, which is
continuous and omni-directional around the wafer.

Focus drift is a process-parameter deviation (Parameter type cause) and is tied to
the focus parameter departing from its target — often reading low relative to best
focus at the edge field.

2. Confirming the cause

Focus telemetry for the exposure tool should be reviewed across the suspect window.
Because focus drift is a parameter deviation rather than a hardware failure, the most
useful checks are telemetry and the negative-control normal-lot ratio, together with
locating the yield change point to bound when the drift began.

Wet Clean Guide — Mechanical Damage
Process Step: CLEAN

1. Scratch defects from megasonic overpower

During wet cleaning, megasonic energy is used to dislodge particles from the wafer
surface. If the megasonic power is set too high, the acoustic cavitation becomes
aggressive enough to damage fragile structures. Excessive megasonic power can induce
micro-scratches, which are occasionally seen at electrical test as a Scratch pattern.

Megasonic overpower is a recipe/method problem (Method type cause) rather than a
worn part, and it is tied to the megasonic power parameter running high. Note that a
Scratch signature is ambiguous: it can originate here in CLEAN (megasonic overpower)
or upstream in CMP (slurry particle contamination), so the two candidate causes must
be weighed against the lot route and telemetry.

2. Confirming the cause

Megasonic power telemetry for the clean tool should be checked first. Because this is
a method/recipe issue, alarm history around the window is relevant, the normal-lot
ratio provides a negative control, and the yield change point bounds the onset.
